questions.subject: Reading
questions.learningObjective: Locate a specific service condition in short everyday notices.
questions.groupInstructions: Enter the notice letter. You may use a letter more than once.
questions.passage:
A. Kiosk parcel collection
Collect prepaid parcels from the kiosk beside the east gate. Bring your collection code. If someone else collects for you, forward them the code before they arrive. The kiosk cannot accept cash payments for orders.

B. Community hall bookings
Residents may reserve the hall for meetings. The hire fee covers chairs and tables. A separate refundable deposit is required if you need a key to the equipment cupboard. Leave the key at reception before claiming the deposit.

C. Riverside shuttle
On Saturday mornings the shuttle leaves from the library entrance because the main stop is used by the produce market. The usual stop reopens at noon. Advance tickets can be moved to a later departure if requested before the time printed on the ticket.

D. Book exchange
The exchange accepts clean books with all pages present. Please remove any slips with your personal details. You may take one book without leaving one. Ask the volunteer for a bag if the books you have chosen are too heavy to carry safely.

E. Tool lending desk
A borrower must attend a short demonstration before taking an electric tool. Hand tools can be borrowed without a demonstration. Tools can be returned through the side window when the main desk is closed, provided an attendant is present.
questions.prompt: Which notice explains how another person can collect something for you?
questions.explanation: A collector can use the code forwarded by the purchaser.

questions.subject: Reading
questions.learningObjective: Use exact words from workplace guidance to complete a paraphrase.
questions.groupInstructions: Complete each sentence using no more than two words from the passage.
questions.passage:
New shift arrangements at a fictional print workshop

On the first day, new staff should meet their shift leader at the loading entrance. The main reception opens later than the production floor. Staff who arrive before their shift leader should remain outside the barrier until someone with access comes to meet them.

A shift exchange begins when both workers enter their agreement in the swap register. A request entered there is provisional. The original arrangement still applies until a supervisor sends written approval. If the exchange is refused because the workers have different machine training, they may ask for a different date.

Before using the cutting machine, check that the work ticket states the required paper size. If the size is absent, put the ticket in the query tray so the production planner can contact the customer. Do not guess from a previous order, even if it appears to be from the same organisation.

At the end of the shift, reusable offcuts go into the sample drawer. Only clean pieces large enough to show the colour and finish should be saved. Write the stock reference on the back of each sample so the next shift can identify it.

A failed job must be recorded on the waste sheet before the spoiled material is discarded. The purpose is to help the workshop tell the difference between material defects and errors in the production process. Staff should describe what they observed, without assigning blame.
questions.prompt: The first meeting with the shift leader takes place at the ______.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph names that entrance as the meeting location.

questions.subject: Reading
questions.learningObjective: Use narrative evidence to distinguish stated facts, contradictions and missing information.
questions.groupInstructions: Answer TRUE if the passage supports the statement, FALSE if it contradicts the statement, or NOT GIVEN if neither applies.
questions.passage:
The things a photograph cannot name

In a fictional town exhibition, a photographer presented images of a bridge before and after its resurfacing. Her earliest photographs were taken to record the progress of the work. They showed the sequence in which old boards were lifted and new ones carried into place. A council officer later invited her to display the pictures in the old ticket hall. She initially planned to arrange the prints by date, with a brief description of the work beneath each one.

While preparing the labels, she showed a trial print to an elderly shopkeeper. He paid little attention to the workers. Instead, he pointed to an umbrella visible beside a pillar and said that the person carrying it used to set up a stall there. The photographer could see neither the person’s face nor any goods in the picture. She wrote down his recollection but decided to keep it separate from what the image itself showed.

A second visitor recalled the same stall in a different place. Rather than settle the matter immediately, the photographer asked each person to describe the landmarks they remembered. The shopkeeper mentioned a pillar with a chipped corner. The second visitor remembered a lamp above a narrow pavement. A later print showed both landmarks, but it did not establish that the stall had stayed in one place. The exhibition eventually printed both accounts on separate cards, each beside the image that prompted it.

On the exhibition’s opening day, visitors were invited to add observations. To avoid losing the link between a comment and its picture, each print had a reference number. Volunteers copied the number onto every new comment card. At the end of the week, the organiser arranged the cards by number before transcribing them. Some visitors supplied possible names for objects, while others recalled movements that a still photograph could never show.

The experiment changed the photographer’s plans for her next project. She would still keep dates and record what was visible. She would also make time to collect differing recollections before writing the final labels. She wanted later viewers to see how an account had been assembled and to notice when its parts were based on different kinds of evidence.
questions.prompt: The photographer’s earliest bridge pictures were intended to document the work as it happened.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph says the earliest photographs recorded the progress of the work.

In a fictional town exhibition, a photographer presented images of a bridge before and after its resurfacing. Her earliest photographs were taken to record the progress of the work. They showed the sequence in which old boards were lifted and new ones carried into place. A council officer later invited her to display the pictures in the old ticket hall. She initially planned to arrange the prints by date, with a brief description of the work beneath each one.

While preparing the labels, she showed a trial print to an elderly shopkeeper. He paid little attention to the workers. Instead, he pointed to an umbrella visible beside a pillar and said that the person carrying it used to set up a stall there. The photographer could see neither the person’s face nor any goods in the picture. She wrote down his recollection but decided to keep it separate from what the image itself showed.

A second visitor recalled the same stall in a different place. Rather than settle the matter immediately, the photographer asked each person to describe the landmarks they remembered. The shopkeeper mentioned a pillar with a chipped corner. The second visitor remembered a lamp above a narrow pavement. A later print showed both landmarks, but it did not establish that the stall had stayed in one place. The exhibition eventually printed both accounts on separate cards, each beside the image that prompted it.

On the exhibition’s opening day, visitors were invited to add observations. To avoid losing the link between a comment and its picture, each print had a reference number. Volunteers copied the number onto every new comment card. At the end of the week, the organiser arranged the cards by number before transcribing them. Some visitors supplied possible names for objects, while others recalled movements that a still photograph could never show.

The experiment changed the photographer’s plans for her next project. She would still keep dates and record what was visible. She would also make time to collect differing recollections before writing the final labels. She wanted later viewers to see how an account had been assembled and to notice when its parts were based on different kinds of evidence.
questions.prompt: The photographer later exhibited the same prints in another town.
questions.explanation: The final paragraph discusses plans for a next project without mentioning a second venue for these prints.
